slides.title: An offline edit vanished without a trace
slides.tldr: When two users edit the same thing offline, whoever syncs last wins and the other's work is lost without anyone being told.

blocks.title: The manager's and the salesman's two ledgers
blocks.body: Ryan, a salesman, goes off on a trip to a rural area with a photocopy of the store's ledger. Back at the store, the manager Kevin changes the same customer's address in the master ledger. When Ryan returns and copies his version over the master, Kevin's entry is wiped out, and nobody ever knows. That is exactly what happens in an offline app.

blocks.caption: Whoever sends last wins: Kevin's change silently disappears

actors.label: Ryan's phone
actors.tip: No signal out on the road, so the change stays stored on the phone.

actors.label: Server
actors.tip: Keeps the one master copy for everybody.

actors.label: Kevin's laptop
actors.tip: Online in the office; changes go to the server immediately.

messages.label: address = "Queens"
messages.tip: Kevin's change landed on the server first.

messages.label: address = "Brooklyn" (back online)
messages.tip: Ryan has no idea Kevin changed it.

blocks.body: Last-write-wins means deleting one person's work without telling anyone.

aside.title: Field-visit notes
aside.body: Field workers at a nonprofit filled in survey forms offline. When two of them edited the same family's record separately, one edit was silently lost at sync, and for weeks nobody noticed.

items.meaning: Write to the phone's own database first, and to the network later.
One change wiping out another without knowing about it.

check.q: Ryan and Kevin both made changes, and the server kept whichever arrived last. What went wrong?
check.a: Kevin's change was lost and nobody knew. That is a lost update: the conflict was never detected, so there was no chance to combine the two edits.

slides.title: Catch the conflict: which version did you write against?
slides.tldr: Send a base version with every change. If the server's version differs, don't write silently: return a 409 conflict and show both copies.

blocks.title: The ledger note "I saw this edition"
blocks.body: The salesman writes "edition 5" on top of his photocopy. When he comes to copy changes into the master ledger, he says "I wrote this after seeing edition 5". If the ledger has meanwhile reached edition 6, the manager says, "Stop, you wrote against an old copy. Look at the new one first." That is **catching** a conflict, not erasing it.

blocks.caption: If the base version doesn't match, the server doesn't write; it answers 409

nodes.label: Ryan's phone
nodes.tip: The phone's copy was edited from v5 and doesn't know what the server has now.

nodes.label: POST /api/sync
nodes.tip: Carries not just the change but also which version it was made against.

nodes.label: notes.version
nodes.tip: The server's true copy. Kevin's edit had already moved it to v6.

nodes.label: 409 Conflict
nodes.tip: Nothing was written. The server's current copy goes back with the reply.

edges.label: The phone sends its change and says it wrote against v5
The server reads the database version: it is v6 now
v5 and v6 differ, so the write must not go through
The server builds a 409 with the v6 copy attached
The phone shows both copies side by side to reconcile

blocks.body: Always send, along with the change, the version you wrote against.

items: With a `#[ORM\Version]` field, Doctrine's optimistic locking bumps the number for you.
A version number isn't clock time, so clock drift can't confuse it.

items.label: Why timestamps don't give the right order

check.q: Why is a version number better than a timestamp for catching conflicts?
check.a: The phone's and the server's clocks don't agree, so a timestamp can give the wrong order. The server bumps the version number itself, so clock errors can't creep in.

slides.title: Five ways to settle a conflict
slides.tldr: LWW is simple but loses data. Field-level merge, asking the user and CRDTs are progressively safer. Choose by the kind of data.

blocks.title: Five rules for reconciling two ledgers
blocks.body: Once a conflict is caught, you need a decision. One rule: whoever signed last wins. Another: address and phone number are separate columns, so keep both people's changes. For hard cases, call both in and ask. And in a stock ledger, write "+2 cartons" instead of "total 10": then any order of merging gives the same result. That is the core idea of a CRDT.

cells: The change that arrives last wins
rows.tip: The simplest, but if you go by the clock, clock errors lose data too. Deciding "last" with a version is better.

cells: Keeps both changes when fields differ
rows.tip: Real conflicts shrink, because most edits touch different fields.

cells: Shows both copies and lets them choose
rows.tip: Where a wrong decision is expensive, it is safest to let a person decide.

cells: Detects concurrent edits via who has seen whose changes
rows.tip: A separate counter per device. If neither of two counters is greater than the other, the two changes are concurrent.

cells: A structure that merges to the same result in any order
rows.tip: The merge rule lives in the structure itself, so conflicts never arise. But you can't build one for every kind of data.

blocks.title: The same stock, two ways
items: Stock is 10 cartons. Offline, Ryan sells 2 and Nicole sells 1.
Send totals: Ryan says 8, Nicole says 9. The last one wins, so stock = 9. The truth is 7.
Send changes: -2 and -1. The server applies both: 10 - 2 - 1 = 7, in any order.
Price: the server must keep every change, and still check the result, because two sales can push stock below 0.

blocks.title: How to choose
items: In an ordinary CRUD app, start here: catch conflicts with a version, merge by field, and show the user what can't be merged.
CRDTs are mainly for documents edited together (Google Docs style). An ordinary app doesn't need that complexity.

items.meaning: Two changes made without either person having seen the other's.
A data structure built so that merging in any order gives the same result.
Peer-to-peer: devices sync directly with each other, with no central server.

use: Money amounts or stock going up and down: send "+2"-style deltas, not the total
avoid: Last-write-wins on money or stock; it gives plainly wrong numbers

check.q: Two people separately changed the same customer's address and phone number. Which way saves both changes?
check.a: Field-level merge. The changes are in two different fields, so both can be kept. With last-write-wins, one change would be lost.

slides.title: Local-first in Vue: write to the phone first, send later
slides.tldr: Save every change to an IndexedDB outbox first, send in order once the network is back, and give each change an id so sending it twice does no harm.

blocks.body: A sync protocol has three steps. When the user edits, write to the phone first, into the **outbox**: a to-do list of changes kept in the browser's own database (IndexedDB), so it survives a closed tab. When back online, `push` the changes in order. Then `pull` the server's new changes. Each change carries its own `id`, so a resend is recognized, and the `baseVersion` it was written against. When the server accepts a change it returns the new version, and the code hands that version to the same note's later edits (the next slide shows why).

marks.tip: A change has its own id and a base version. The server uses both, to catch duplicates and to catch conflicts.
Write to the phone's IndexedDB first. Even with no network, the change isn't lost.
On any failure other than 409 (server down) the outbox stays as it is and is tried again later.
On a 409 the edit moves to conflicts together with every later edit of the same note. None is retried.
Accepted: the later edits of this note now say they were written against the version the server just returned.

items.meaning: A small database built into the browser. It keeps data after the tab is closed.
The phone's to-do list of changes that the server has not yet accepted.

items: `navigator.onLine` is only a guess. The real truth is whether a fetch succeeds.
Add Background Sync or a Service Worker and the outbox drains even when the tab is closed.
Keep the outbox only in memory and offline changes are lost the moment the tab closes.

check.q: Why give every change an id with `crypto.randomUUID()`?
check.a: If the connection drops and the reply is lost, the client sends the same change again. The server recognizes the id, knows it was already applied, and doesn't write it twice.

slides.title: Your own second edit can conflict with your first
slides.tldr: Two offline edits of one note both say "written against v5". After the first is accepted the second looks stale, so rebase it onto the new version.

blocks.body: Out on the road Ryan edits one note's title twice, and the phone has only ever seen version 5. So both edits go out saying "I wrote this against v5". The first is accepted and the server moves to v6. The second then arrives still saying v5, and the server refuses it. Nobody else touched the note: Ryan has conflicted with himself.

blocks.caption: Without rebasing, edit 2 is refused because of edit 1

actors.label: Ryan's phone
actors.tip: Holds two waiting edits of the same note, both written while the phone knew only v5.

actors.label: Server
actors.tip: Accepts a change only if its base version equals the note's current version.

messages.note: Offline: edit 1 and edit 2, both base v5

messages.label: Edit 1 (base v5)
messages.tip: The server's note is v5 too, so this one matches.

messages.label: Applied, the note is now v6
Edit 2 (base v5)
messages.tip: The phone never updated edit 2 after edit 1 was accepted.

messages.label: 409: you wrote on v5, I am at v6

messages.note: Ryan is in conflict with himself

blocks.caption: With rebasing, edit 2 follows edit 1 and goes through

actors.label: Ryan's phone
actors.tip: After each accepted edit it rewrites the base version of the waiting edits of that note.

actors.label: Server
actors.tip: Same rule as before: base version must equal the current version.

messages.label: Applied, the note is now v6

messages.note: Rebase: edit 2 now says base v6

messages.label: Edit 2 (base v6)
messages.tip: It now matches the server's version.

messages.label: Applied, the note is now v7

blocks.title: The rules, and their price
items: After the server accepts an edit, copy the version it returned into every later edit of that note.
If an edit gets 409, park the later edits of that note too: they were built on top of it.
Price: one note's edits go out one at a time, and a parked chain waits until the user settles it.

items.meaning: Re-point a waiting edit at the newest version, as if it had been written after the edit just accepted.

use: Several edits of one note can queue up offline
avoid: Never guess the next version on the phone (base + 1) while offline: if Kevin also edited, you would overwrite him

check.q: Edit 1 was accepted and the server says v6. Edit 2 still says base v5. What does the phone do before sending it?
check.a: It rebases: it sets edit 2's base to the v6 the server returned. Without that, the server answers 409 and Ryan conflicts with himself.

slides.title: The Symfony server: match the version, send changes back
slides.tldr: The server spots duplicates by mutation id, matches the base version with a Doctrine optimistic lock, and on a mismatch answers 409 with its own copy.

marks.tip: With `#[ORM\Version]`, Doctrine bumps and checks the version on every UPDATE.
With LockMode::OPTIMISTIC and the expected version, Doctrine throws right here if the client's base version doesn't match.
We only get here because the version didn't match. Send the client the server's copy; nothing was written.

items: For pull, build `GET /api/changes?since=<cursor>`, where the cursor is a server-side counter that keeps growing, not a clock.
Record `applied->record()` in the same transaction as the data change. It stores the version the edit produced (`baseVersion + 1`), so a resend gets the same answer.
Every reply that accepts an edit, `applied` or `duplicate`, carries the version: the client needs it to rebase its next edit.

check.q: Why does the server send its own copy with the 409, not just "conflict"?
check.a: The client needs the server's current data to show the two copies side by side and merge them. Told only "conflict", the user can't do anything.

slides.title: "Is it ready?" "Not yet." Every two seconds
slides.tldr: If every client asks the server about an order's status every 2 seconds, almost every request comes back empty, yet each one costs the server full price.

blocks.title: Asking again and again at the coffee shop
blocks.body: Fifteen customers walk up to the counter every minute asking "is my coffee ready?". The person at the counter is worn out answering, and the real work stalls. If the shop simply called out order numbers or used a buzzer, nobody would need to ask. Polling is the first way; **push** is the second.

blocks.caption: 10,000 users, each with an order that changes 3 times an hour

items.label: Polling (2s)
items.tip: 10,000 users / 2 seconds. Almost all of these are "nothing changed" answers.

items.label: Push
items.tip: 10,000 x 3 changes / 3,600 seconds. A message goes out only on a real change.

blocks.body: Instead of asking again and again, let the server tell you when something changes.

aside.title: Live scores on game night
aside.body: A sports site polled every second for live scores. In the final game traffic grew 20 times, the database buckled, and the site went down at the very moment the score changed.

items.meaning: The client asks the server at fixed intervals.
The server tells the client on its own whenever something changes.

check.q: If 10,000 users poll every 2 seconds, how many requests per second reach the server, and why is that wasteful?
check.a: 5,000 per second. Almost all are "nothing changed" answers, yet the server runs the full request for each one.

slides.title: Polling, long-polling, SSE, WebSocket
slides.tldr: For one-way news from server to browser, SSE is simple and enough. Reach for WebSocket only when both sides talk a lot.

blocks.title: Four ways the coffee shop gives news
blocks.body: **Polling**: the customer keeps asking. **Long-polling**: the customer says "call me when the coffee's ready" and stands waiting, then stands there again after being called. **SSE**: the shop's loudspeaker; the server broadcasts one way. **WebSocket**: a phone call, where both sides can speak any time.

blocks.caption: The four connection types side by side

rows.tip: SSE goes one way only: server to browser. To send from browser to server, an ordinary POST does the job.
SSE is plain HTTP, so proxies, auth and load balancers work as before. WebSocket brings a separate protocol.

cells: The browser does it, with Last-Event-ID
rows.tip: When an SSE connection drops, the browser reconnects itself and sends the last event id, so missed messages come back.
Most business apps need the "server will tell you" kind, where SSE is enough.

blocks.title: Which to pick
items: The server only announces (order status, feeds, notifications): SSE.
Frequent messages in both directions (chat, games, co-editing): WebSocket.
The user isn't in the app: push notification (FCM or Web Push), since there is no open connection then.

use: SSE: on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, dozens of connections are no problem
avoid: WebSocket: overkill just to say "your order was created"

items: On HTTP/1.1 a browser allows only 6 connections per domain; open 6 SSE tabs and everything stalls. HTTP/2 fixes this.

check.q: You need to push an order's status from server to browser. SSE or WebSocket, and why?
check.a: SSE. The messages flow one way (server to browser), it runs over plain HTTP, and the browser handles reconnect and Last-Event-ID itself. WebSocket's complexity would be extra here.

slides.title: Symfony Mercure: publishing from the server
slides.tldr: A Mercure hub holds the SSE connections. Symfony just publishes an Update through HubInterface, and a cookie grants access to private topics.

blocks.body: PHP-FPM wasn't built to keep many connections open. So a separate **Mercure hub** (written in Go, also built into FrankenPHP) holds them. Symfony only tells the hub "send this data on this topic", and the hub passes it to every subscriber. For personal data, mark the update `private` and authorize each user only for their own topic.

marks.tip: A topic is a URL-style name. Only those who subscribed to this name receive the update.
`private: true` means only authorized subscribers get it; nobody without a JWT can see it.
First, Symfony's own voter checks: does this order belong to this user?
The subscriber JWT goes into a cookie. It grants access to this one topic only.

items: Publish only after the main transaction has committed. That is why this lives in a Messenger handler.
The hub is one more service to run. Symfony publishes to it with a secret (`MERCURE_JWT_SECRET`) and a URL (`MERCURE_URL`); the Flex recipe sets both up.
If the SPA runs on a different domain, set the cookie's domain and `SameSite` right, or the hub won't receive the cookie.

check.q: What can happen if you publish a Mercure update without `private: true`?
check.a: Anyone who knows the topic name can subscribe and watch other people's order updates. With private, the hub checks that the subscriber's JWT grants access to the topic.

slides.title: EventSource in Vue: listen, and don't forget to close
slides.tldr: First fetch the current state with a plain GET, then listen to live changes with EventSource. Call close() on unmount so connections don't pile up.

blocks.body: When the page opens, a plain GET brings in the order's current state, and `EventSource` then listens for new changes. But the stream only carries changes made after it opens, and a change between the first load and the moment it opens is gone. The same holds after a dropped connection, unless the hub keeps history and is set up to replay it. So every time the stream opens, fetch the current state again. And when the component goes away, close the connection yourself.

marks.tip: A plain GET returns the true state right now, whatever messages were missed before or between connections.
Without `withCredentials` the browser doesn't send the cookie, and the private topic isn't authorized.
Every open, first or after a reconnect, re-reads the current state. That closes the gap the stream cannot cover.
If the connection drops, the browser reconnects itself and sends Last-Event-ID; the hub replays missed updates only if it keeps history.
Without close(), the connection stays open after the page changes and they keep piling up.

items: Forget `close()` on unmount and every visit to the page leaves one more connection behind.
Don't rely on EventSource alone: it cannot bring back what happened before it opened. Re-fetch the state on every open.
To listen to several topics, add the `topic` parameter more than once; you still need only one connection.
A refresh answer can arrive after a newer message. For fields that can move backwards, send a version number and ignore older ones.

check.q: What happens if you don't call `source.close()` when the component unmounts?
check.a: The connection stays open after the user leaves the page, and each visit adds another. Both the browser's limit and the server's memory get eaten away.

slides.title: The price of connections: scaling, presence and push
slides.tldr: Every open connection costs server resources. The hub receives once and sends to many. Presence is a heartbeat plus a TTL, and push notifications cover users outside the app.

blocks.caption: Publish once, and the hub spreads it over thousands of connections

nodes.label: Symfony app
nodes.tip: On a domain event it informs the hub once. Holding connections open is not its job.

nodes.label: Mercure hub
nodes.tip: Lightweight and efficient with concurrent connections. It keeps thousands of them in a single process.

nodes.label: Browsers
nodes.tip: Each browser holds one open HTTP connection.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.tip: The record of who is online, with a TTL.

nodes.label: FCM / Web Push
nodes.tip: There is no connection, so the message goes through the phone OS's own channel.

edges.label: The app publishes once, with a topic
The hub sends the message to every subscribed browser
Each browser pings every 30s; the app renews a Redis key with a 60s TTL
If the user is offline, it sends through a push provider

blocks.title: Three calculations
items: **Scaling**: every connection holds a socket and memory. PHP-FPM with 50 workers is full at 50 connections; a hub holds tens of thousands.
**Presence**: who is online, via heartbeats. When the TTL runs out the key disappears, and the server assumes the user is gone.
**Push notification**: with the app closed there is no connection, so go through the OS (FCM, Web Push). The user must allow it; delivery isn't guaranteed.

blocks.body: Holding connections and doing the work are separate duties. Keep them on separate servers.

items: Don't measure presence by "is the connection open" alone. On mobile, connections die silently, so you need a heartbeat and a TTL.
Even after a push notification, fetch the current state from the server when the user opens the app; don't trust the push message.

check.q: Why isn't checking whether the connection is open enough to know if a user is online?
check.a: A mobile network can drop silently while the server still thinks the connection is open. With a heartbeat and a TTL, no regular reply means "offline".

slides.title: Opening the feed stitches together 1,000 people's posts
slides.tldr: If every feed view searches for "all posts from the people I follow", that one query is what chokes the site as users grow.

blocks.title: The newsstand vs the paper carrier
blocks.body: In the newsstand model, the reader walks around 1,000 newsstands every morning, hunting for the pieces they like. In the paper-carrier model, the moment an article is printed, the paper carrier drops it at the reader's door. Feed design is a choice between the two: should the work happen at **read time** or at **write time**?

blocks.code:
-- runs every time the feed is opened
SELECT p.*
FROM posts p
JOIN follows f ON f.followee_id = p.author_id
WHERE f.follower_id = 7
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

marks.tip: If the user follows 1,000 people, the database wades through all 1,000 people's posts just to pick the newest 20.
To sort, it must first collect every matching row. As data grows, this is what gets slow.

blocks.body: A feed is read many times more often than it is written, so make the read path cheap.

aside.title: The slow page of year one
aside.body: A social app ran fine on this JOIN in its first year. Once users passed 2 million, the feed query reached 3 seconds and the database CPU sat at 100% all day.

items.meaning: A time-ordered list of posts from the people a user follows.
Spreading something one person creates to many people.
Asking the database to match rows from two tables, here every follow with the posts of the person followed.

check.q: Why is running that JOIN on every feed open harmful, even though the query is correct?
check.a: Both the follow counts and the posts keep growing, and opening the feed is the most frequent action. A huge join-and-sort every time makes the database buckle.

slides.title: Write-time vs read-time fan-out
slides.tldr: Write-time puts a post into every follower's feed as it is written, so reads are cheap. Read-time stitches the feed together on read, so writes are cheap.

blocks.title: The paper carrier and the newsstand
blocks.body: In the paper-carrier way (**write-time**), when a new issue comes out the carrier drops 200 copies at 200 subscribers' doors. Printing day is hard work, but the moment a subscriber sits down to read, the paper is ready. In the newsstand way (**read-time**), nothing happens at printing, but every reader has to go around collecting it each time.

blocks.caption: The trade-offs of the two ways

columns.title: Write-time (push)
items: Feed reads are very fast: one list from one key
Write cost grows with the number of followers
More space: a separate copy per person
With many followers, the write itself is a burden
columns.tip: When a post is created it is put into every follower's feed. Opening a feed means reading one ready-made list.

columns.title: Read-time (pull)
items: Writes are cheap: the post is stored once
Feed reads are slow: joined every time
No extra space needed
Whoever follows the most people gets the slowest feed
columns.tip: The post is written only once. On opening the feed, new posts from everyone you follow are joined and sorted.

blocks.title: How to think about it
items: When reads dominate (nearly every social feed), do extra work at write time to make reads cheap.
When reads are rare and writes frequent (logs, weekly reports), read-time is the right one.
Example: 100,000 posts a day x 200 followers = 20 million list inserts, about 230 a second.
In return, each of 1 million feed opens reads one ready list instead of searching 200 people's posts.

aside.body: Paper carrier = write-time: hard work first, reading is easy. Newsstand = read-time: printing is easy, reading is hard.

check.q: Most users post rarely but open their feed many times. Which fan-out suits them?
check.a: Write-time. Reads far outnumber writes, so doing the work once at write time to make every read cheap pays off.

slides.title: The celebrity problem: one post, 5 million writes
slides.tldr: With write-time fan-out, one post from a celebrity with 5 million followers makes 5 million writes. The fix is hybrid: push posts from ordinary users, pull the celebrity's at feed-read time.

blocks.caption: Writes per post under write-time, at 10,000 writes a second

items.label: Ordinary
items.tip: 200 feed writes take about 0.02 seconds. Nobody notices.

items.label: Popular
items.tip: 20,000 writes take about 2 seconds of the workers' time. Heavy, but fine.

items.label: Celebrity
items.tip: 5 million writes take 500 seconds, over 8 minutes. Everyone else's posts wait in the queue behind it.

blocks.body: This is the **hot key** problem: one user can jam the entire system. The fix is **hybrid**. For users whose follower count is below a threshold (say 10,000), put their posts into followers' feeds at write time. Don't fan out celebrities' posts at all. When a feed is opened, fetch the recent posts of the celebrities that user follows directly, and merge them into the user's own feed.
Push the ordinary users' posts; pull the celebrity's at read time and merge.

blocks.title: What hybrid costs
items: Opening a feed now also asks the posts table about each celebrity the user follows, and runs one more merge step.
Keep that cheap: cache each celebrity's latest posts once, shared by all their followers.
Not worth it when nobody has more than a few thousand followers: plain write-time is simpler.

use: Hybrid: when follower counts differ hugely (social, news)
avoid: Hybrid: when everyone has similar follower counts; then plain write-time is simple and enough

items: Set the threshold once and forget it, and feeds break as users cross it; keep watching follower counts.

check.q: Why does hybrid not write a celebrity's post into followers' feeds?
check.a: One post would mean 5 million writes, filling the queue and holding up everyone else's posts. So it is stored once and merged in when the feed is read.

slides.title: Fan-out in chunks with Messenger
slides.tldr: Fan-out is huge work, so break it up: each message takes 1,000 followers, writes to Redis, then dispatches the next chunk. If a message runs twice, the feed stays correct.

blocks.body: When a post is saved, a `FanOutPost` message goes out. The handler takes 1,000 followers, adds the post id to each one's Redis **sorted set** (a list ordered by a score, here the time), then dispatches a message for the next 1,000. Why chunks: one message for 10,000 followers that crashes at follower 6,000 must redo all 10,000, while with chunks it redoes at most 1,000. Running `ZADD` again with the same member and score changes nothing, so redelivery does no harm.

marks.tip: 1,000 followers after the last id seen. No OFFSET, so it stays fast even on a huge list.
ZADD is idempotent: adding the same (post, time) again creates no duplicate in the feed.
We keep at most 800 items per feed. Older ones come from the database when needed.
The next chunk's message carries a checkpoint (the last follower id). If it breaks midway, work resumes from there.

items: The Redis feed is really a cache: if lost, it can be rebuilt from the posts table, where the true data lives.
For a celebrity's post, don't dispatch `FanOutPost` at all; past the threshold, let it live in the posts table only.

items.meaning: A Redis list where every item has a score and the list stays sorted by it.
Sending many Redis commands in one trip instead of one trip each.

check.q: If the fan-out handler runs twice on redelivery, why doesn't the same post appear twice in the feed?
check.a: Giving a sorted set the same member again with `ZADD` doesn't create a new row, it only updates the score. The member is the postId, so a duplicate has nowhere to go.

slides.title: Reading the feed: merge, and keep the order stable
slides.tldr: Feed = the user's precomputed list + the new posts of the celebrities they follow, merged by (time, id). Page with a (time, id) cursor, not an offset and not time alone.

blocks.caption: The path when a feed opens: two sources, one sorted list

nodes.label: User
nodes.tip: Asks for the first or the next chunk of the page, with a cursor.

nodes.label: Feed API
nodes.tip: Combines the results of both sources and sorts them by time and id.

nodes.label: Redis feed
nodes.tip: The post ids of ordinary followees, placed there at write time.

nodes.label: Posts table
nodes.tip: The recent posts of the celebrities this user follows come from here.

edges.label: The user asks for the feed, with the previous page's cursor
It reads 20 ids from its own feed, those after the cursor
It fetches the older posts of the followed celebrities
It merges, sorts by time and id, and sends the best 20

blocks.body: A cursor made of the time alone has a hole. Say posts 9, 8 and 7 landed in the same millisecond and a page holds 2. Page 1 is posts 9 and 8, the cursor says "older than that millisecond", and post 7 is never shown. So the cursor is the pair (time, id): "older, or the same time with a smaller id". Ties are rare on one page, but over millions of page turns they happen every day.

marks.tip: Redis lists tied posts in text order, not number order. So read every post at the cursor's millisecond and filter by id in PHP.
`(` means "less than" (exclusive): only strictly older milliseconds here, because the ties were handled above.
Posts at the same time are ordered by id, so the order is the same on every page turn.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, created_at_ms
FROM posts
WHERE author_id IN (:stars)
  AND (created_at_ms, id) < (:at, :id)   -- time first, id breaks the tie
ORDER BY created_at_ms DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- first page: bind :at and :id to the largest values

marks.tip: A row comparison: older time, or the same time with a smaller id. A time-only `<` here would drop the posts that share the boundary millisecond.

items: A cursor of the time alone drops every post that shares the last millisecond of the previous page.
Deleted or blocked posts stay in the feed; when reading, filter them by checking the true state in the posts table.
Give the client the cursor as one opaque string (such as `1700000000123_9`). Price: no jumping straight to page 7, only next and previous.
The feed is eventually consistent: a post reaches followers' feeds a few seconds later. That is acceptable, but show the author their own post immediately.

check.q: Why does the cursor hold both the time and the id, rather than the time alone?
check.a: Posts can share a millisecond. With time alone, the ones that did not fit on the page are skipped on the next one. The id decides who comes after whom.
